The relentless sun beat down upon the yard, bleaching the very dust to a fine white powder. Eleonora heaved at the stubborn axle of the cartwheel, her breath coming in short, frustrated gasps. Her hair had escaped its pins, sticking in damp tendrils to her brow, and a smudge of grease adorned one cheek. The task was beyond her, yet it had to be done.

From the shade of the verandah, a faint voice reached her. "A noble effort, Nora. Truly Herculean. Do be careful you don't break a nail."

She did not turn her head. "If you have the energy for jests, Julian, you have the energy to fetch me the larger wrench."

"Alas, my energy is purely of the intellectual sort," he returned, his tone one of lazy amusement. "Besides, it is far more entertaining to watch."

A sound of hooves made her pause, her hand still upon the grimy wheel. She felt a familiar tightening in her chest even before she looked up to see him. Alistair rode into the yard as if he were a part of the harsh landscape itself, his expression unreadable. He dismounted in one fluid motion, his eyes taking in the scene, lingering for a fraction of a second on her dishevelled state before moving to the broken cart.

He said nothing at all. He simply walked over, took the spanner from her unresisting fingers, and set it aside. The silence was more damning than any rebuke.

"The men are all out at the north pasture," she said, her voice thin and defensive. "It needed mending before the supply run."

He did not seem to hear. He braced himself, his shoulder muscles bunching under his cotton shirt, and with a single, powerful wrench, he freed the axle. The metallic groan was loud in the still air. He worked for some minutes, his movements economical and sure, while she stood by, feeling useless and strangely small. The action was a statement in itself. It was as if he had corrected a child's clumsy scrawl with a firm, masculine hand.

When he was done, he straightened up and wiped his hands on a rag from his saddlebag. Only then did he look at her fully. "Go inside," he said. His voice was low, yet it held the quality of an order that would not be questioned.

She stiffened. "I have things to do. Julian's lunch must be prepared."

"Let the cook prepare it. That is her job."

"Mary is preparing the evening meal. I cannot ask her to do everything." She felt the hot colour rise in her cheeks under his scrutiny. His gaze was so steady; it seemed to strip away all her paltry excuses.

"And you can?" he asked, a hard edge to his tone. "You can be nurse, cook, and mechanic all at once? Look at your hands."

She instinctively hid them behind her back. A sudden tremor went through her, born of heat and exhaustion and the sheer force of his presence. "They are my hands, to do with as I please."

He took a step closer. "Nora, stop this foolishness." It was not a plea; it was a command. He put a hand on her arm, his grip firm but not rough. "You have done more than enough. You have been wearing yourself to a shadow for months."

"Julian needs me," she whispered, her eyes falling away from his.

"Julian is recovering," he said flatly. "He will not perish if his lunch is served ten minutes late by a paid servant. You, however, are another matter." He paused, his thumb moving almost unconsciously against her arm. The small caress sent a shock through her that was utterly unnerving. "I am riding to the upper weir this afternoon. You will come with me."

Her head shot up. "I cannot! To leave Julian for so long? It is out of the question!"

Across the small space between them she met his look, and she saw the inflexible purpose there. "I insist," he said.

She drew a shaky breath, feeling her defences crumble. "Why must you always be so… so autocratic?"

"Because you will not listen to reason," he returned, without a flicker of apology. "Because someone has to consider you, since you plainly will not consider yourself. Does my wish mean nothing to you?"

The question, so quietly put, disarmed her completely. "Of course it does," she faltered. "You know it does. But my duty…"

"Your duty is done," he interrupted. "For this afternoon, at least. Will you come?"

She looked from his resolute face to the cool, dark doorway of the house where she knew a hundred small tasks awaited her. Yet the thought of the open air, of the ride beside him, pulled at her with an astonishing force. She felt trapped between what she ought to do, and what her heart cried out for.

"Very well," she said, her voice barely audible. "If you wish it."

He let go of her arm, but the sensation of his touch remained. "I do wish it," he said simply. "Go and rest until then. That is not a request."

"You have no right," she managed at last, her voice thin and unsteady. "You have no right to say such a thing to me. My life is my own."

"Is it?" he returned, his tone dangerously soft. "You have given it entirely to Guy. You have made yourself his slave. Do you think I haven't seen? Do you think I haven't watched you wearing yourself to a shadow, day after day, while he grows stronger? You do not eat. You do not sleep. You are a ghost of the woman who came to this farm."

Every word was true, and the truth of it was a lash against her pride. She tried to pull her arm free, but his grip was like iron. "He is my brother," she said, her voice choked with a mixture of anger and despair. "I owe him my care."

"You have paid that debt ten times over," Burke said, his gaze never leaving her face. "Now you owe something to yourself. And," he paused, his eyes darkening, "you owe something to me."

The world seemed to tilt on its axis. "To you?" she whispered, staring at him, utterly bewildered. "What could I possibly owe to you?"

He did not answer immediately. His gaze held hers, so fierce and compelling that she could not look away. It was as if he were trying to pour all his unspoken thoughts, all his long-held frustrations, directly into her soul. She felt a tremor run through her, a response to something she had refused to acknowledge for months.

"You owe me the consideration you would give to any friend," he said at last, his voice rough with some suppressed emotion. "You owe me the peace of mind of knowing you are not driving yourself into your grave. That is what I ask of you, Sylvia. No more, for now."

He released her so abruptly that she staggered back a step. The place on her arm where his hand had been felt suddenly cold. He turned away from her, breaking the spell.

"Lunch is ready," he said, his voice once more gruff and impersonal. "Go and eat. We will ride at three."

She stood there, her heart hammering against her ribs, while he moved to the sideboard and poured two glasses of water. He did not look at her again. He had said his piece, and for him, the matter was settled. She watched him, a tumult of emotions warring within her. Resentment fought with a strange, unwilling gratitude. His high-handedness was infuriating; yet, underneath it, she felt the solid bedrock of his concern, a thing she had leaned upon more than she had ever admitted.

She went to the table and sat down, her limbs feeling strangely weak. He brought the glasses and set one before her. They ate the cold beef and salad which Mary Ann had left for them in near-total silence. Sylvia was acutely aware of his presence across the small table. She could feel his eyes on her whenever her own were fixed on her plate, but when she glanced up, he was always looking elsewhere. The air between them was thick with unspoken things. His declaration hung there, a tangible force that had altered the very shape of their world. He would not stand by and watch her. He had laid claim to her well-being, whether she willed it or not. The thought was both terrifying and profoundly comforting.

After the meal, he rose. "Go and rest," he said. It was the same command he had given her outside, and this time she had no spirit to argue. She was exhausted to the very marrow of her bones. She nodded mutely and went to her room.

The small chamber was hot and stuffy, but she barely noticed. She sank down onto her bed, not bothering to draw the curtains. She lay staring up at the ceiling, Burke's words echoing in her mind. You owe something to me. What had he meant by it? Was it merely the concern of a friend, as he had claimed? Or was it something more, something she had glimpsed in the depths of his eyes and steadfastly ignored? Her thoughts were a hopeless tangle. She felt as if she had been walking a narrow, clearly-marked path for months, a path of duty and devotion to Guy. Now, Burke had suddenly appeared and, with a few forceful words, had pointed out another path, one that led into an unknown country. And he was not inviting her to walk it; he was commanding her to.

She thought of his hands, so strong and capable, finishing the work of setting up the camp-bed with a few deft movements. She thought of his gaze, which stripped away all her defences. A slow, unwilling warmth spread through her. For so long, she had been the one who was strong, the one who took charge. To have someone else, for a moment, take the burden from her was a relief so profound it bordered on pain.

She must have slept, for she was startled by a light tap on her door. "Sylvia?" It was Burke's voice, low and resonant. "It is three o'clock."

She sat up, feeling groggy but also strangely refreshed. The deep, dreamless sleep had done its work. "I'm coming," she called, her voice still thick with slumber.

She splashed her face with water from the basin and hurriedly changed into her riding habit. As she pinned her hat in place, she caught sight of her reflection in the small, freckled mirror. Burke was right. Her face was pale and thin, and there were dark shadows under her eyes that no amount of sleep could instantly erase. She looked ill. The realisation came with a small shock of surprise. She had been so focused on Guy that she had not truly looked at herself for months.

When she went out, Burke was waiting by the horses. He had saddled her mare himself. He turned as she approached, and his eyes swept over her in a quick, assessing glance. He did not smile, but she thought she saw a flicker of approval in his expression.

"Feeling better?" he asked.

"Yes, thank you. I slept."

"Good." He gave her a leg up into the saddle, his hand firm and impersonal at her elbow. "Guy knows we are going. He told me to tell you to enjoy yourself."

She settled herself in the saddle, gathering the reins. "What did he say?" she asked, a little nervously.

Burke swung himself onto his own mount. "He said," he replied, his mouth twitching almost imperceptibly, "that it was about time someone took you in hand. He seems to approve of my methods."

The hot colour flooded Sylvia's cheeks. She urged her mare forward without a reply, intensely aware of Burke riding silently beside her. They left the cluster of farm buildings behind and struck out across the veldt. The sun was still hot, but a slight breeze had sprung up, stirring the long, dry grass. The sky was a vast, brilliant blue, stretching to the hazy line of the mountains in the distance. For a long time, neither of them spoke. There was a comfort in the silence, in the rhythmic creak of leather and the soft thud of hooves on the baked earth.

Sylvia felt the tension of the past weeks begin to drain out of her. Out here, under the immense sky, the worries of the sickroom seemed to shrink and recede. The world was bigger than Guy's room, bigger than the farm. She had almost forgotten.

"I have not ridden this way for a long time," she said at last, more to herself than to him.

"I know," he said simply.

They rode on, climbing steadily. The path grew narrower, winding between great sun-warmed boulders. Burke rode ahead to lead the way. She watched his straight back, the easy way he sat his horse. He seemed a part of this landscape, as rugged and enduring as the land itself. He belonged here. And she? She had always felt like a visitor, a temporary resident whose real life was elsewhere. But lately, she had found it harder and harder to imagine what that other life might be.

He stopped at a high point and waited for her to draw alongside. Below them, the farm was a miniature collection of roofs nestled amongst trees.

"It looks so peaceful from here," she murmured.

"It is," he said. "The trouble is all in your head, Sylvia."

She turned to look at him, stung by the remark. "That is not fair. Guy was desperately ill."

"He was," he agreed. "But he is not now. The crisis is past. You must learn to let go. For his sake as much as for yours. He will never be a man again if you persist in treating him as a helpless child."

She knew he was right. Guy himself had chafed at her constant fussing. Yet the habit of anxiety was hard to break. "I will try," she said quietly.

"See that you do," he said, but his tone was less harsh now. He pointed towards a distant green smudge on the landscape. "There are the Merstons'. Not much further now."

They continued on their way, and as they rode, he began to talk. He spoke of the farm, of his plans for the next season, of the new breed of sheep he intended to buy. He spoke as an equal, seeking her opinion on matters of irrigation and pasture. She found herself drawn into the conversation, her mind, so long preoccupied with thermometers and medicine schedules, slowly engaging with these larger, healthier problems. She felt a part of his world, of his future, and the feeling was a heady one.

By the time they reached the Merstons' homestead, she was feeling more like her old self than she had in a year. Mrs. Merston, a stout, kindly woman with a face as weathered and pleasant as a ripe apple, came out to greet them.

"Sylvia, my dear girl! It's been an age. Burke, you rogue, why have you been hiding her away?" She enveloped Sylvia in a hug that smelled of lavender and freshly baked bread. "Goodness, child, you're thin as a rake! We need to fatten you up."

Sylvia laughed, feeling the last of her reserve melt away under the woman's uncomplicated kindness. "I am fine, Mrs. Merston. It is good to see you."

"Fine, she says!" Mrs. Merston held her at arm's length, her shrewd eyes taking in the pale cheeks and shadowed eyes. "Burke, I hope you are taking proper care of this girl. She looks as if she's been working herself to death."

"I am doing my best, Kate," Burke said, a faint smile touching his lips. "That is why I brought her here. She needs a change of scenery."

They were ushered inside for tea. While Mr. Merston and Burke talked of cattle prices, Kate Merston fussed over Sylvia, pressing cake and sandwiches upon her and keeping up a cheerful stream of local gossip. It was all so normal, so wonderfully mundane. Sylvia found herself relaxing completely, laughing at the older woman's stories and answering her gentle questions about Guy's recovery. She saw Burke glance at her once or twice from across the room, his expression unreadable, but she was no longer discomfited by his scrutiny.

All too soon, it was time to leave. As they stood by the horses, Mrs. Merston took Sylvia's hand. "You come and see me more often, my dear. Don't let these men work you so hard. And you," she said, turning a stern eye on Burke, "you see that she does."

"I will," Burke promised.

The ride home was quieter. The sun was low in the sky, casting long shadows across the veldt and painting the mountains in hues of rose and violet. A profound sense of peace settled over Sylvia. The afternoon had been a gift, a respite she had not known how desperately she needed.

"Thank you, Burke," she said, as they neared the farm. "I was wrong. I needed to get away."

"I am not often wrong about such things," he said, without a trace of arrogance. It was a simple statement of fact.

They rode the last stretch in a companionable silence. When they reached the stables, Joe came running to take the horses. Burke dismounted and came to her side, holding up his hands to help her down. She placed her hands on his shoulders, and for a moment, as he lifted her down, she was held close against him. His strength was a solid, reassuring reality. Her heart gave a sudden, wild leap. He held her for a second longer than was necessary, his face very close to hers in the gathering dusk.

She could feel his breath on her cheek. "Sylvia," he said, his voice a low vibration that seemed to run through her entire body.

"Yes?" she whispered, unable to move, unable to breathe.

He did not kiss her. He simply looked at her, his gaze intense and searching, as it had been in the sitting-room. Then he gently set her on her feet and stepped back.

"You have colour in your cheeks," he said, his voice once more controlled. "That is better."

She could not speak. She felt dazed, as if she had just woken from a powerful dream. He walked with her to the door of the house. The lamps had been lit inside, casting a warm yellow glow into the twilight.

"Go and have your dinner," he said. "And then I want you to go to bed. Mary Ann can sit with Guy if he needs anything. He doesn't, but it will make you feel better."

"Burke," she began, not knowing what she wanted to say.

He put a hand on her arm, stopping her. His touch was light, but it sent a shock of awareness through her. "There is no need for words. Just do as I say. For tonight."

She looked up at him, at his strong, unsmiling face, and saw the inflexible will there. But she also saw something else, something deeper and more vulnerable, which he guarded so fiercely. It was in the taut line of his jaw, in the depths of his dark eyes.

"Very well," she said softly. "Good night."

"Good night, Sylvia."

He did not move until she had gone inside and closed the door. She leaned against it for a moment, her eyes closed, her senses reeling. She heard his footsteps recede, firm and steady on the hard-packed earth.

She went through the motions of eating dinner with Guy, who was in high spirits and teased her gently about her outing. She answered his questions and smiled at his jokes, but her mind was elsewhere. It was with Burke. It was re-living the pressure of his hands on her, the intensity of his gaze, the low timbre of his voice.

Later, as she lay in her bed, the house quiet around her, she knew that something had irrevocably shifted. Burke had taken control, not just of her afternoon, but of her life. He had turned a page in the book, just as Guy had done with his cigarette, and bade her not to look back. And she found, to her own astonishment, that she had no desire to. The path of duty had been safe, but it had also been a prison. Burke was leading her into the unknown, and for the first time in a very long while, she felt not dread, but a thrilling, terrifying flicker of hope.

"That's no answer," he said, though his tone was gentle. He looked past her to Burke. "Is she happy, Burke? That's all that matters. You'd better have made damn sure of that."

"I intend to spend the rest of my life making sure of it," Burke replied quietly. "I have asked Sylvia to be my wife."

Guy was silent for a moment. He pushed the tray away and leaned back against the pillows, his eyes closing briefly. When he opened them again, his gaze was clear. "I see," he said. He managed a faint, crooked smile. "Well. I can't say I'm surprised. Only that it took you both so confoundedly long."

He held out a hand, not to Burke, but to his sister. She went to him, dropping to her knees beside the bed and taking his hand. It felt thin and frail in hers.

"You're not… angry?" she asked in a low voice.

"Angry?" He gave a short, mirthless laugh. "Good heavens, no. Relieved, if you want the honest truth. I've been a millstone around your neck for years, Sylly. It's time someone cut the rope." His eyes met Burke's over her bent head. "You're a good man, Burke. Better than me. You'll be good to her."

"That is my sole intention," Burke said.

"Good." Guy's gaze returned to his sister. He squeezed her hand. "Now stop looking like a frightened rabbit. You've earned this. Go and be happy. Lord knows, it's overdue." He released her hand and waved a dismissive gesture towards the door. "And for pity's sake, go and have your lunch. You're making me feel like the villain in a melodrama, and I haven't the strength for it."

Sylvia rose to her feet, wiping her eyes with the back of her hand. Burke put a steadying arm around her shoulders. She looked down at her brother, her heart a tangle of gratitude, relief, and a lingering, sorrowful ache. He had come back, indeed. But he was a different Guy from the one she had known. The boy was gone, and in his place was a man who had looked into the abyss and carried the shadow of it in his eyes.

"We will talk more later," Burke said to him. "There are plans to be made."

"Plans," Guy echoed, with a flicker of irony. "Yes. There are always plans. Don't worry about me. I'm not about to fade away. I might even get up for dinner."

They left him then, and as they walked back to the sitting-room, Sylvia felt the tension of the last hour begin to ebb away, leaving her weak but strangely peaceful. Burke led her to a chair and gently pushed her into it.

"Sit," he commanded. "I will fetch the food. You are not to move a muscle."

She watched him go, his tall frame filling the doorway. He was her rock, her harbour. He was her future. The thought was still so new, so staggering, that she could hardly encompass it.

He returned in a few moments with a tray, which he set on a small table before her. He had brought her soup, and bread, and a glass of wine. He sat opposite her, not eating himself, but watching her with an intentness that was both unnerving and deeply comforting.

"You must eat," he said.

Obediently, she picked up her spoon. The soup was hot and nourishing. She had not realised how hungry she was. As the warmth spread through her, she felt her strength returning.

"What did you mean," she asked after a while, "when you said there were plans to be made?"

"I mean," he said, leaning forward, "that we will be married as soon as it can be arranged. I will ride into Brennerstadt tomorrow and speak to the padre. There is no reason to wait, Sylvia."

"But the farm," she protested automatically. "And Guy…"

"The farm will be here," he said patiently. "And Guy, as he said himself, will be all right. We will find a good manager to run this place. Or we will sell it. It doesn't matter. My place is large enough for all of us, and more. Or we can go away. We can go anywhere you wish. To England, if you like."

England. The word conjured a dim, half-forgotten world of green fields and grey skies. A world she had left behind so long ago. She looked at him, at his strong, sun-browned face, and knew that she did not want that world. This was her world now. This harsh, beautiful land.

"No," she said softly. "I don't want to go to England. I want to stay here. With you."

The fierce light of joy that leaped into his eyes was all the reward she could have asked for. He reached across the table and took her hand.

"Then we will stay," he said. "We will build our life here. Together."

The future, which had for so long been a terrifying, formless fog, began to take shape before her eyes. It was a future of shared burdens and shared joys. A future of waking up beside him, of riding with him across the veld, of building a home. A future where love was not a duty, but a gift.

She finished her soup in silence, her mind busy with these new and wonderful thoughts. When she was done, he took the tray away, and then came to stand behind her chair. His hands rested on her shoulders, their warmth seeping through the thin fabric of her dress.

"You are tired," he said. "I want you to rest this afternoon."

"But the ride to the Merstons," she remembered.

He chuckled, a low, pleasant sound. "I think the Merstons can wait. I have other plans for this afternoon. I plan to sit here, on the stoep, and watch over my future wife while she sleeps. It is a new occupation for me, and one I think I shall enjoy very much."

She twisted in her chair to look up at him, a real smile, free of all anxiety, finally reaching her eyes. "You are absurd."

"I am in love," he corrected her gravely. "It is a condition which, you will find, leads to a great deal of absurdity."

He bent down and kissed the top of her head. "Go on," he urged gently. "I have put the long-chair on the stoep. The afternoon is cool. Rest now, my Sylvia. Our life begins tomorrow."

And as she went, obediently, out into the dappled sunlight of the stoep, she knew that he was right. The long night was over. A new day, bright with unimaginable promise, was about to dawn.
